paragraphs: A man who has finally found something to do will not need a new suit for it. His old one will do, even if it has been lying dusty in the attic for a long time. Old shoes will last a hero longer than his servant, if a hero ever has a servant. Bare feet are older than shoes, and he can manage with them. Only people who go to evening parties and parliament need new coats, which they change as often as they change themselves. But if my jacket and trousers, my hat and shoes are good enough to worship God in, they will do, won't they? Who has ever worn out a coat so completely that it could not still be given to a poor boy? He might pass it on to someone poorer still, or perhaps richer, since he could manage with less. Beware of every enterprise that requires new clothes rather than a new person inside them. If there is no new man, how can the new clothes fit? If you have an enterprise ahead of you, try it in your old clothes. People want not something to do things with, but something to do, or rather something to be. Perhaps we should never buy a new suit, however torn or dirty the old one, until we have acted or sailed in some way and feel like new men inside it. Keeping it then would be like keeping new wine in old bottles. Like the moulting season of birds, our time of change must be a crisis in our lives. The loon goes away to lonely ponds to spend it. In the same way, the snake throws off its skin and the caterpillar its coat, by effort and growth from inside. Clothes are only our outer skin. Otherwise we will be living a lie, and in the end both we and the rest of mankind will judge us badly.

We put on one piece of clothing after another, as if we grew like some plants by adding layers outside. Our outer clothes, often thin and fancy, are a false skin. They are not part of our life and can be removed without serious harm. Our thicker everyday clothes are like a plant's inner layer. But our shirts are our true bark, and removing it all around would kill the man. I believe all peoples wear something like a shirt at times. A man should dress so simply that he can find himself in the dark. He should live so compactly and be so prepared that, if an enemy takes the town, he can walk out of the gate empty-handed and calm, like the old philosopher. One thick garment is usually as good as three thin ones, and cheap clothing is easy to find. A thick coat costs five dollars and lasts five years. Thick trousers cost two dollars, leather boots a dollar and a half, a summer hat a quarter of a dollar, and a winter cap sixty-two and a half cents, or a better one can be made at home for almost nothing. So where is the man so poor that, wearing such a suit paid for by his own work, he will not find wise men to respect him?
